_doc: Hand-curated organizations (Michiko, 2026-11-01). Each org's members, roles and citations are set here and win over the automatic org finder. 'drop' lists automatic labels whose members are replaced by these curated lists. Curated orgs are always shown, even with zero or one member.

orgs.name: Vigilant Committee to suppress crime (1822)
orgs.note: An anti-crime, law-and-order committee formed in 1822, with Richard Allen as chairman and Russell Parrott as secretary (Poulson's, March 2, 1822). A different body from the later vigilance committees that aided fugitives. Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. The Philadelphia Inquirer (Mar. 6, 1822) reported it as a committee of vigilance, thirty in number, appointed at a numerous meeting at Bethel Church to co-operate with the Mayor and police (Newspapers.com clipping). Clipping: clippings/PI_1822-03-06_p2_committee-of-vigilance.jpg

orgs.name: Committee of Vigilance to support the Rights of All (1829)
orgs.note: Appointed at a meeting chaired by Benjamin Paschal Jr. to support Samuel Cornish's newspaper The Rights of All (Rights of All, Oct. 9, 1829). Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries.

orgs.name: Vigilant Committee of Philadelphia (1837)
orgs.note: Founded in 1837 to aid people escaping slavery. Winch's sources call it both the Vigilance Committee and the Vigilance Association: James McCrummell president (later Robert Purvis), James Needham treasurer, Jacob White secretary, with a standing committee. Active into the 1840s. Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. Dr. James J. G. Bias is linked from Winch notes that are filed under Eliza A. Bias but describe him (cupper, later dentist, 2 Acorn Alley).

orgs.name: Female Vigilant Committee
orgs.note: The Female Vigilant Association of Philadelphia, founded 1838: Elizabeth White president, Sarah McCrummell treasurer, Ruth Harding secretary (Pennsylvania Freeman, July 5, 1838). It raised money and aid alongside the men's Vigilant Committee but was its own organization. Charles W. Gardner addressed it in 1840.

members.r: meeting held at her home, 169 Pine

orgs.name: Special Vigilance Committee (1851)
orgs.note: Formed in late 1851, after the Christiana resistance, to aid fugitives (Frederick Douglass' Paper, Nov. 13, 1851; Voice of the Fugitive, Jan. 15 and Feb. 12, 1852). Members as listed in Julie Winch's reference entries. Its report on the Christiana cases, signed by Nath'l W. Depee, Secretary, Feb. 10, 1852, and printed in Frederick Douglass' Paper, March 4, 1852 (p. 1, col. 3), shows it hiring legal counsel for the Christiana defendants, supporting the 25 prisoners through four months in jail, aiding their families, sending Geo. Williams and Jacob Moore and their families to Canada, and boarding the witnesses during the trials. It raised $689.41 from Philadelphia churches (Bethel gave $73.50) and beneficial societies, and from donors as far as San Francisco. Courtesy New York Heritage Digital Collections, St. John Fisher University. Clipping: clippings/FDP_1852-03-04_p1_special-vigilance-committee-report-detail.jpg

orgs.name: Vigilance Committee of 1852 (William Still)
orgs.note: The committee William Still worked through after 1852, as remembered by William Carl Bolivar (Pencil Pusher Points, Philadelphia Tribune, Aug. 23, 1913): John P. Burr, Rev. Jeremiah Asher, N. Depee, William Still, I. C. Wear, Jacob C. White and Charles Wise.

orgs.name: Frank Johnson Guards
orgs.note: A Black militia company in Philadelphia. In 1859 it assembled and marched armed through the city. Amos Webber described the march in his diary, and the Daily Ledger objected that only white men could legally keep military companies; a Baltimore Sun article also covered it. No members are on record yet. Source: 1838 Black Metropolis blog post on Samuel Williams, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/post/williams

orgs.name: Williams Assembly (1865)
orgs.note: Founded in 1865 by Samuel Williams specifically for protection. Its constitution speaks of 'protection' rather than the 'mutual relief' of ordinary beneficial societies; members were barred from gambling, profanity and public drunkenness, and it had a Marshall and bought badges, at a time when no Black man could join the Philadelphia police (until William Dicks in 1884). Source: 1838 Black Metropolis blog post on Samuel Williams, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/post/williams

orgs.name: Agricultural and Mechanics Association of Pennsylvania and New Jersey
orgs.note: A Black-led stock association founded in Philadelphia on May 1, 1839, with $10 shares. Its constitution allowed the treasurer to put share money toward buying land, stock, materials and fixtures, and toward agents and teachers. Jacob C. White Sr. kept its stock book and accounts and served as treasurer. Many of its subscribers were also active in the Vigilant Committee and the Female Vigilant Committee. Source: constitution and stock book, Leon Gardiner Collection, Historical Society of Pennsylvania; 1838 Black Metropolis blog, https://www.1838blackmetropolis.com/site/post/finding-black-led-creation-and-use-of-economic-instruments-to-support-freedom-seekers-in-1840/

orgs.name: Committee of Vigilance against kidnapping (1827)
orgs.note: Appointed at Bethel Church in February 1827, after Richard Allen read the congregation Mayor Joseph Watson's notice about Philadelphia children kidnapped and sold into slavery in the South: 'a committee of vigilance consisting of twenty persons of colour... to aid in the detection of those offenders, and to give all and every necessary information to the civil authorities of this city.' A public meeting at Bethel on Monday, Feb. 5, 1827 took up the abductions. Its twenty members are not named in the report. Sources: United States Gazette, Feb. 23, 1827, p. 4; Philadelphia Inquirer, Feb. 3 and 5, 1827 (Newspapers.com clippings, 1838 Black Metropolis).
